title: Next.js caching & revalidation: Cache Components
objectives: Explain the Next.js 16 default (with `cacheComponents`, nothing is cached until `use cache`) and what changed from Next 14 and 15
Write a `use cache` function with `cacheLife` and `cacheTag`, reading `cookies()`/`headers()` outside the cached scope and passing values in as arguments
Choose `updateTag`, `revalidateTag(tag, "max")`, `revalidatePath` or `refresh` after a write, from where it runs and who must see the change
Predict what a `cacheLife` profile does over time: `stale` (client router), `revalidate` (background regeneration), `expire` (blocking), defaults and nesting
Explain why a local `next start` doesn't prove how production caches, and read cache behaviour on the real platform instead

sources.title: Next.js docs: Caching and Revalidating (Previous Model)

questions.prompt: Next.js 16 with `cacheComponents: true`. A Server Component awaits a database query and has no `use cache` anywhere above it. When does the query run?

options.text: On every request, and the component must sit inside `<Suspense>` or the build fails with a blocking-route error (uncached data accessed outside of `<Suspense>`)
Once at build time; the result is reused until you revalidate
Once, then cached for the default 15 minutes
On the first request, then cached until a deploy

questions.explanation: Under Cache Components caching is entirely opt-in: uncached work runs at request time. Because it can't be part of the prerendered shell, Next requires you to say where it streams (a `<Suspense>` boundary) or to cache it (`use cache`). "Cached at build by default" is the Next 14 habit; the 15-minute figure is the `default` profile, which applies only **inside** `use cache`.

questions.prompt: A page written for Next 14 reads `searchParams` (so it renders on every request) and calls `fetch(url)` with no options, relying on Next 14 serving that fetch from its Data Cache. After upgrading to Next 15 or 16 (without Cache Components), what happens?

options.text: The fetch is no longer cached by default, so the upstream API is called on every request until you opt in
Nothing changes; `fetch` caching is a web-platform default
The build fails until each fetch declares a `cache` option
It's now cached forever, until a deploy

questions.explanation: Next 15 changed the default: `fetch` requests (and `GET` Route Handlers) are no longer cached. In the previous model you opt back in with `cache: "force-cache"`, `next: { revalidate }` or `fetchCache`; under Cache Components you wrap the work in `use cache`. The browser's HTTP cache has nothing to do with the Next server's fetch cache. (On a page with no request-time APIs, Next 15+ still prerenders the route, so there the fetch runs once, at build.)

questions.prompt: A `use cache` function needs the visitor's currency, stored in a cookie. What's the right shape?

options.text: Read `cookies()` in an uncached caller and pass the currency string in as an argument
Call `await cookies()` inside the cached function; Next adds the cookie to the key
Pass the `cookies()` promise in as an argument and await it inside
Switch to `cacheLife("seconds")` so a stale currency doesn't matter

questions.explanation: Cached scopes can't touch request APIs: calling `cookies()` inside throws, and passing the unresolved promise makes `next build` wait on request data that doesn't exist until it times out. Await outside, pass the **value**: arguments are part of the cache key, so each currency gets its own entry. A shorter `cacheLife` fixes nothing here: the problem is where the cookie is read, not how long the result lives.

questions.prompt: Inside `async function Orders({ userId })`, a nested `const load = async (status) => { "use cache"; return db.orders(userId, status) }` is called. Do two users share one cached result?

options.text: No: `userId` is captured from the closure, and captured variables become part of the key
Yes: only the explicit argument `status` is in the key, so user B sees user A's orders
Nothing is cached, because nested functions can't use `use cache`
It throws, because closures can't be serialised

questions.explanation: The `use cache` docs: variables referenced from outer scopes are captured and bound as arguments, so they join the key alongside the explicit ones. That's what makes per-user caching safe. The real leaks come from what the key can't see: shared module state, or data fetched with credentials that aren't part of the inputs.

questions.prompt: In a Server Action, a user saves their display name, then `redirect("/profile")`. The profile reads data tagged `user-42`. Which call guarantees the redirected page shows the new name?

options.text: `updateTag("user-42")`
`revalidateTag("user-42", "max")`
`refresh()`
None needed: a redirect always renders fresh data

questions.explanation: `updateTag` expires the entries so the next read waits for fresh data: read-your-own-writes, Server Actions only. `revalidateTag(tag, "max")` is stale-while-revalidate, so the very next render may still show the old name. `refresh()` re-renders without touching cached data, and a redirect alone doesn't invalidate anything.

questions.prompt: A CMS calls your Route Handler `POST /api/cms-webhook` when an article is published. How should it invalidate `post-<slug>`?

options.text: `revalidateTag("post-" + slug, "max")`
`updateTag("post-" + slug)`
`refresh()`
`revalidateTag("post-" + slug)`

questions.explanation: `updateTag` and `refresh` are Server Action–only and throw in a Route Handler. The one-argument `revalidateTag` is deprecated in Next 16. With `"max"`, the next visitor gets the cached article instantly while the new one is built in the background, which is fine when nobody is waiting on their own write. (If the CMS needs the old copy gone at once, the docs show `{ expire: 0 }`.)

questions.prompt: `/blog` and `/dashboard` both show posts fetched with the `posts` tag. A Server Action calls `revalidatePath("/blog")`. What does `/dashboard` show on its next visit?

options.text: Its cached copy: only `/blog` was invalidated, and the `posts` tag wasn't
Fresh posts, because they share the tag
An error, because the two pages are now out of sync
Fresh posts, because `revalidatePath` clears the whole server cache

questions.explanation: The `revalidatePath` docs use exactly this example: the path is refreshed, but other pages using the same tags keep serving cached data until those tags are invalidated. Tags describe **data**, paths describe **pages**; when the data changed, invalidate the tag. (`revalidatePath("/", "layout")` is the deliberate everything switch.)

questions.prompt: `getProducts()` uses `cacheLife("hours")` (revalidate 1 hour, expire 1 day) and was cached at 09:00. Traffic is steady. What does a request at 10:10 get?

options.text: The 09:00 result immediately, while the server regenerates it in the background for later requests
It waits while the server regenerates, then gets fresh data
The 09:00 result, and nothing regenerates until the 1-day expire
Whatever the browser cached: `revalidate` is the browser's timer

questions.explanation: Past `revalidate`, Next serves the cached entry and regenerates it in the background (stale-while-revalidate), so this visitor is fast and the next one sees new data. A request **waits** only past `expire`, which counts time without traffic. The browser's timer is `stale`, a separate number (5 minutes in every built-in profile except `seconds`).

questions.prompt: The build output lists `/sitemap.xml` with a 4-hour revalidate, and on `next start` it regenerates on schedule. Someone reports production serving yesterday's sitemap. What settles it?

options.text: Read production: `x-vercel-cache` / `age` and a date in the body, some hours after the last deploy
The local run: `next start` is the production server, so the report is wrong
The build output table, which is generated from the same config
Run `next dev` and watch it regenerate

questions.explanation: A local production build is evidence about Next's server. The deployed platform adds its own storage and CDN (on Vercel, a per-deployment ISR cache behind a CDN), and that is what visitors get. `next dev` is further still from production: it never runs the build-time prerender. A finding measured on production can only be overturned by measuring production.

prompts.prompt: Turn on Next.js 16's opt-in caching model.
prompts.explanation: `cacheComponents` (Next 16) replaces the Next 15 experiments `experimental.dynamicIO` / `experimental.useCache` and `experimental.ppr`. Without it, the previous model's `fetch` options and segment config still apply.

prompts.prompt: Cache this query for hours and tag it so a write can invalidate it.
prompts.explanation: The directive goes first in the function body. `cacheLife` and `cacheTag` (no `unstable_` prefix since Next 16) must run inside the cached scope; calling `cacheLife` at module level throws.

prompts.prompt: Invalidate the same tag from a Server Action (the writer must see it at once) and from a CMS webhook Route Handler.
prompts.explanation: `updateTag` gives read-your-own-writes and exists only in Server Actions. In a Route Handler you use `revalidateTag` with a profile; `"max"` is the recommended stale-while-revalidate choice.

prompts.prompt: Read the cookie outside the cache and hand the cached component a plain value.
code: async function PriceList({ currency }: { currency: string }) {
prompts.explanation: `cookies()` is async (synchronous access was removed in Next 16) and must stay outside the cached scope. The awaited string becomes a prop, and props are part of the cache key, so each currency is cached separately.

code: redirect("/posts"); // /posts lists posts read with cacheTag("posts")
snippets.question: Is the new post in the list the author lands on?
snippets.answer: Not necessarily: that render can be served the stale list while a fresh one regenerates in the background
acceptable: maybe not; it shows the stale list
snippets.explanation: `revalidateTag(tag, "max")` marks the entries stale; the next visit gets stale-while-revalidate: the old copy immediately, the new one for whoever comes after. That's right for a CMS update nobody is watching and wrong for the person who just clicked Save. `updateTag("posts")` exists for this case: it expires the entries so the redirected render waits for fresh data.

snippets.question: How often does Dashboard's cached output revalidate?
snippets.answer: Every 15 minutes (the default profile); the inner hour can't lengthen it
snippets.explanation: An outer `use cache` without its own `cacheLife` runs on `default` (revalidate 15 minutes). Inner caches with a **shorter** lifetime pull it down; a **longer** one, like this hour, can't extend it. Had Widget used `cacheLife("minutes")`, Dashboard would revalidate every minute. Writing an explicit `cacheLife` on the outer scope makes it win either way, which is why the docs recommend it.

code: // The user opens /feed, clicks a <Link> to /about,
// and 2 minutes later clicks a <Link> back to /feed.
snippets.question: The server's copy is past `revalidate`. Does the browser ask the server for /feed again?
snippets.answer: No: the client router reuses its copy until `stale` (5 minutes) runs out; `revalidate` is the server's timer
acceptable: no, it uses the client cache
snippets.explanation: `stale` controls Next's client router cache (sent as `x-nextjs-stale-time`), not HTTP headers; `revalidate` and `expire` are about the server. Two minutes in, the server would regenerate on its next request, but the browser doesn't send one: it shows the copy it already has until 5 minutes have passed. The router also never honours a `stale` below 30 seconds. A Server Action that calls `updateTag`, `revalidateTag`, `revalidatePath` or `refresh` clears the client cache outright, which is how a write still shows up immediately.
